Date: 2026-10-24 (Europe/Zurich)
Baseline: main, 8dde94a7e261f0e05c42dfe334686cfee288086f
Candidate: SIMD implementation, 4d8d4ece23bf25513173fa1932b21dab30a7e975
Toolchain: go1.27.3 windows/amd64, GOAMD64=v1, CGO_ENABLED=0
OS: Windows build 26300.9711
CPU: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-11800H @ 2.30 GHz; 16 logical CPUs
Power plan: Balanced (381b4222-f694-41f0-9685-ff5bb260df2e)
Runtime feature probe using simd/archsimd:
  runtime=go1.27.3-X:simd windows/amd64 CPUs=16 AVX=true AVX2=true
  Features checked with archsimd.X86.AVX() and archsimd.X86.AVX2().
Both computers execute the same AVX implementation; there is no AVX2-specific
kernel in this candidate. Cross-machine ratios measure the whole computers.

Builds: go test -c -pgo=off -o <binary>
  main.txt: baseline production sources, GOEXPERIMENT unset
  main-experiment.txt: baseline production sources, GOEXPERIMENT=simd
  simd.txt: candidate production sources, GOEXPERIMENT=simd
GOFLAGS, GODEBUG and GOMAXPROCS unset during timing; -test.cpu=1 sets one Go CPU.
No explicit OS CPU affinity. No tests, builds, linting, or other benchmark
commands were run concurrently with the benchmarks.

Sources were extracted with git archive into separate temporary directories.
The candidate's benchmark_test.go and squeeze_simd_test.go were copied into
both directories, along with identical temporary digest-reporting tests.
Production sources were unchanged. All binaries ran from the working repository
root, using its CRLF fixture files, rather than the LF files in the archives.
fixture-digests.txt records the byte length and SHA-256 of each source fixture;
input-digests.txt records the length and SHA-256 of each assembled corpus.
The seeded random generator and all benchmark data match the earlier harness.
Despite its name, mixed-256k has 812032 bytes, tiny-text has 3200 bytes, and the
other corpora have 262144 bytes.

Benchmark command for each sample:
  <binary> -test.run=^$ -test.bench=^BenchmarkPureGoGzip$ -test.benchtime=2x -test.count=1 -test.cpu=1

Six samples per build, using the same permutations as the i7-3610QM run:
  main, main-experiment, simd
  simd, main-experiment, main
  main-experiment, simd, main
  main, simd, main-experiment
  simd, main, main-experiment
  main-experiment, main, simd
run-order.txt records UTC timestamps for each invocation. End-to-end benchmarks
ran from 08:39:53 to 08:43:34 UTC (10:39:53 to 10:43:34 Europe/Zurich).

DefaultOptions: 15 optimal-parsing iterations, block splitting enabled.
Each sample has two timed compressions plus Go's untimed calibration invocation.
Medians are the arithmetic mean of the third and fourth sorted samples.
All samples are retained; there is no outlier removal.

Median default gzip compression time (milliseconds):
Corpus             Main       Main+experiment  SIMD       Saved vs main
tiny-text            10.66       9.96              8.30       22.1%
mixed-256k         1802.39    2936.84           1518.12       15.8%
web-assets-256k     627.06     668.45            428.66       31.6%
records-logs-256k   708.02     744.20            501.32       29.2%
real-files-256k     624.64     666.89            439.39       29.7%
random-256k         121.44     121.59            120.63        0.7%
Saved = 100 * (1 - median SIMD / median main), using unrounded medians.

Observed sample ranges (milliseconds, minimum to maximum):
Corpus             Main                 SIMD
tiny-text            10.09 -   11.08        8.12 -    8.64
mixed-256k         1787.49 - 1856.31     1493.16 - 1705.16
web-assets-256k     613.59 -  647.12      427.42 -  456.39
records-logs-256k   691.85 -  732.17      495.34 -  512.33
real-files-256k     617.27 -  679.75      432.05 -  445.16
random-256k         119.47 -  129.34      117.26 -  125.11
Random data's 0.7% median difference is within this observed variation.

The main+experiment control is 62.9% slower than ordinary main on mixed-256k.
Every control sample is slower (2870.85-3069.80 ms) than every ordinary-main
sample (1787.49-1856.31 ms). The source and build settings were checked; the
cause has not been isolated. SIMD saves 48.3% against that control, but the
headline 15.8% uses ordinary main, as in the earlier computer's comparison.
The other compressible corpora save 16.6-35.9% against the experiment control.

Comparison with the saved i7-3610QM results in the parent directory:
Corpus             Old saved vs main  New saved vs main  Old SIMD / new SIMD
tiny-text               13.8%              22.1%              2.03x
mixed-256k              15.9%              15.8%              1.79x
web-assets-256k         26.5%              31.6%              1.88x
records-logs-256k       23.2%              29.2%              1.92x
real-files-256k         25.7%              29.7%              1.88x
random-256k             -0.6%               0.7%              2.00x
Both runs use Go 1.27.3, Windows/amd64, GOAMD64=v1, PGO off, the same baseline,
six samples of two operations, one Go CPU and the same build-order permutations.

Focused scan benchmarks (main-scan.txt, simd-scan.txt), run sequentially after
the end-to-end benchmarks:
  <binary> -test.run=^$ -test.bench=^BenchmarkFirstImprovableLength$ -test.benchtime=200ms -test.count=6 -test.cpu=1
The 256-entry no-hit scan has median 99.400 ns on main and 50.075 ns with SIMD
(1.99x faster), compared with 177.000 ns and 93.475 ns (1.89x) on the i7-3610QM.
Short and early-hit scans can regress: length-256/hit-0 is 1.019 ns on main
versus 8.994 ns with SIMD. End-to-end measurements include this overhead.

Validation:
  All timed benchmark invocations passed gzip round-trip checks.
  Allocated bytes and allocation counts are identical across all three builds
    for every corpus and every sample, and match the older computer's results.
  main-digests.txt, main-experiment-digests.txt and simd-digests.txt match exactly.
    Each contains default and fast gzip output SHA-256 digests for all six
    corpora, plus the generated fixture in gzip, zlib and deflate formats for
    both profiles (18 digests per build).
  Those 18 digests also match ../main-digests.txt and ../simd-digests.txt.
  Full test suite output is retained in validation.txt:
    go test -pgo=off -count=1 ./...
    GOEXPERIMENT=simd go test -pgo=off -count=1 ./...
    GOEXPERIMENT=simd GODEBUG=cpu.avx=off go test -pgo=off -count=1 ./...
  Environment-variable prefixes above are shell-independent notation; in
    PowerShell set the corresponding $env: variables before running Go.

Follow-up AVX2 experiment:
  avx2-broadcast/ records a guarded BroadcastFloat64x4 prototype compared with
  this AVX implementation, including its exact candidate patch and new timings.
  A runtime probe during that follow-up found that Windows Go 1.27.3 ignores
  GODEBUG CPU feature overrides: AVX and AVX2 remain true with cpu.avx=off and
  cpu.avx2=off. The earlier command labelled simd-fallback in validation.txt
  passed, but did not exercise the fallback. The follow-up uses temporary source
  overrides to exercise the AVX and scalar paths explicitly. See its metadata
  and forced-fallback-validation.txt for the corrected coverage.

Follow-up AVX2 cost-update experiments:
  avx2-relax/ records three relaxStatLengths prototypes against the AVX2
  broadcast baseline, with exact patches, fresh profiling, focused benchmarks,
  initial and confirmation compression runs, and fallback validation.
  Four-lane cost calculations with scalar winning-length writes save 6.2% and
  6.0% on mixed-256k in the two runs. Packing eight length writes is not a
  convincing end-to-end win; inlining the scalar fallback is inconclusive.
  See avx2-relax/metadata.txt for ranges, limitations and reproduction commands.
